frames.summary: Router Advertisement from fe80::a00:27ff:fe00:1 (lifetime 1800s, preference medium, DNS fe80::a00:27ff:fe00:1)

alerts.title: ARP claim contradicts a trusted IPv4 binding
alerts.explain: Frame 37 says 192.168.56.1 is at kali (08:00:27:00:00:66), but the sensor already knows 192.168.56.1 belongs to router (08:00:27:00:00:01) (learned from DHCP server identifier, frame 19). ARP has no authentication, and RFC 826 tells every host that already has 192.168.56.1 cached to overwrite it with the sender's MAC. That is how one forged reply redirects traffic. Nobody asked for this reply (unsolicited).

alerts.title: One MAC address claims several IPv4 addresses
alerts.explain: kali (08:00:27:00:00:66) has now claimed 2 different IPv4 addresses (192.168.56.1, 192.168.56.66). A normal client owns one address on a LAN. An attacker sitting in the middle claims the gateway and the victim at the same time.

alerts.title: A host now trusts the attacker
alerts.explain: After frame 37, ubuntu-client's IPv4 gateway resolves to kali (08:00:27:00:00:66) instead of the real router, router (08:00:27:00:00:01). Its traffic for that role now goes through another machine.

alerts.explain: Frame 44 says fe80::a00:27ff:fe00:1 is at kali (08:00:27:00:00:66), but the sensor learned fe80::a00:27ff:fe00:1 belongs to router (08:00:27:00:00:01) (from RA from the trusted router, frame 23). frames.summary: Router Advertisement from fe80::a00:27ff:fe00:66 (lifetime 1800s, preference high, DNS fe80::a00:27ff:fe00:66)

alerts.title: Router Advertisement from an untrusted device
alerts.field: Ethernet source / RA Source Link-Layer Address option
alerts.explain: kali (08:00:27:00:00:66) is announcing itself as an IPv6 router (lifetime 1800s, preference high). Only router (08:00:27:00:00:01) is the real router. Any host can send an RA and every host that hears it adds the sender to its default-router list (RFC 3756, section 4.2.1). With a higher preference it wins outright.

alerts.title: Router Advertisement hands out an untrusted DNS server
alerts.explain: The RA in frame 45 carries an RDNSS option naming fe80::a00:27ff:fe00:66 as the DNS server. Hosts that accept RDNSS (RFC 8106) will send name lookups there, so the attacker can answer with any address it likes.

frames.summary: DHCPv6 ADVERTISE from fe80::a00:27ff:fe00:66, DNS fe80::a00:27ff:fe00:66

alerts.title: DHCPv6 server reply from an untrusted device
alerts.explain: kali (08:00:27:00:00:66) sent a DHCPv6 ADVERTISE naming fe80::a00:27ff:fe00:66 as the DNS server. Only router (08:00:27:00:00:01) is trusted to answer. DHCPv6 replies are not authenticated, so whoever answers a Solicit first can set the client's IPv6 DNS server.

ARP-01.title: ARP claim contradicts a trusted IPv4 binding
ARP-01.explain: Frame {i} says {ip} is at {claimed}, but the sensor already knows {ip} belongs to {expected} (learned from {source}). ARP has no authentication, and RFC 826 tells every host that already has {ip} cached to overwrite it with the sender's MAC. That is how one forged reply redirects traffic.

ARP-02.title: One MAC address claims several IPv4 addresses
ARP-02.explain: {claimed} has now claimed {count} different IPv4 addresses ({ips}). A normal client owns one address on a LAN. An attacker sitting in the middle claims the gateway and the victim at the same time.

ND-01.title: Neighbor Advertisement contradicts a trusted IPv6 binding
ND-01.explain: Frame {i} says {ip} is at {claimed}, but the sensor learned {ip} belongs to {expected} (from {source}). The Override flag is {override}. RFC 4861 tells a host to replace its cached link-layer address when O=1, which is the IPv6 version of ARP poisoning (RFC 3756, section 4.1.1).

RA-01.title: Router Advertisement from an untrusted device
RA-01.explain: {claimed} is announcing itself as an IPv6 router (lifetime {lifetime}s, preference {pref}). Only {expected} is the real router. Any host can send an RA and every host that hears it adds the sender to its default-router list (RFC 3756, section 4.2.1). With a higher preference it wins outright.
RA-01.field: Ethernet source / RA Source Link-Layer Address option

RA-02.title: Router Advertisement hands out an untrusted DNS server
RA-02.explain: The RA in frame {i} carries an RDNSS option naming {dns} as the DNS server. Hosts that accept RDNSS (RFC 8106) will send name lookups there, so the attacker can answer with any address it likes.

DHCP-01.title: DHCPv4 server reply from an untrusted device
DHCP-01.explain: {claimed} sent a DHCP {msg}. Only {expected} is the trusted DHCP server. Clients take the first offer they get, so a rogue server can set the victim's gateway and DNS server.

DHCP-02.title: DHCPv4 lease points at an unexpected gateway or DNS server
DHCP-02.explain: This lease tells {client} to use gateway {router} and DNS {dns}. Earlier leases on this network used gateway {base_router} and DNS {base_dns}.

D6-01.title: DHCPv6 server reply from an untrusted device
D6-01.explain: {claimed} sent a DHCPv6 {msg} naming {dns} as the DNS server. Only {expected} is trusted to answer. DHCPv6 replies are not authenticated, so whoever answers a Solicit first can set the client's IPv6 DNS server.

D6-02.title: DHCPv6 server on a network with no IPv6 router
D6-02.explain: No legitimate Router Advertisement has been seen, so this network looks IPv4-only, yet a DHCPv6 server just answered. Windows asks for DHCPv6 by default and prefers IPv6 DNS, which is exactly the gap mitm6 abuses [6].

XP-01.title: A host now trusts the attacker
XP-01.explain: After frame {i}, {host}'s {what} resolves to {actual} instead of the real router, {expected}. Its traffic for that role now goes through another machine.
